title: 05. Load Balancing & Scalability: Sticky Sessions
summary: Sticky Sessions (session affinity) route all requests from the same client to the same backend, established via a cookie, IP hash, or session ID — preserving per-client server-side state at the cost of uneven load and…
objectives: What are sticky sessions, and what problem do they solve?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Sticky Sessions (session affinity) route all requests from the same client to the same backend, established via a cookie, IP hash, or session ID — preserving per-client server-side state at the cost of uneven load and lost-session-on-failover.

Stateless services are easy to load-balance: any backend can serve any request, so RR or LC spreads load evenly and a backend failure just causes a retry elsewhere. Stateful services are harder: if the backend holds per-client state — a shopping cart in memory, a WebSocket connection, a half-completed file upload, a session-scoped CSRF token, a JIT-compiled user-specific lookup table — sending the client's next request to a different backend breaks the workflow. The state is on backend A, but the request lands on backend B; B has no idea what A was doing. Sticky sessions solve this by pinning each client to one backend: the first request goes to whatever the LB picks (RR, LC, etc.), and subsequent requests from the same client are routed to the same backend, so the server-side state stays where the client expects it.

The mechanism for "pinning" varies. **Cookie-based stickiness** is the most common: on the first request, the LB injects a `Set-Cookie: SERVERID=backend3` header into the response; on subsequent requests, the client sends `Cookie: SERVERID=backend3`, and the LB reads it and routes to backend3. AWS ALB's sticky cookies (`lb_cookie`) and HAProxy's `cookie` directive work this way. **Application-cookie stickiness** uses a cookie the application itself sets (e.g., `JSESSIONID` for Java/Tomcat, `connect.sid` for Node/Express) — the LB learns the mapping from cookie value to backend by observing the first response, then routes subsequent requests with the same cookie to the same backend. **IP-hash stickiness** hashes the client's source IP and uses the hash to pick a backend — no cookie needed, works for clients that don't support cookies, but breaks when clients are behind NAT (a corporate office of 1000 users all appear as one IP, all pinned to one backend, instantly saturating it). **Session-ID stickiness** uses an application-generated session ID embedded in the URL (`/api/cart;jsessionid=ABC123`) or header — the LB reads the session ID and routes accordingly.

The trade-off of sticky sessions is fundamental: **uneven load and failover state loss.** Uneven load arises because clients are not evenly distributed — a power user with 10,000 requests/hour is pinned to one backend, which becomes a hotspot, while 100 casual users spread across the other backends. IP-hash is worst (one corporate NAT = one backend), cookie-stickiness is better (each client is one entry), but neither matches the even distribution of plain RR. The mitigations are partial: consistent hashing (so adding/removing a backend only re-maps 1/N of clients) and load-aware stickiness (so the LB can break stickiness for an over-loaded backend, at the cost of losing session state for those clients). Failover state loss is the bigger problem: when a sticky backend fails, all its pinned clients are re-routed to other backends that don't have their state — shopping carts vanish, WebSocket connections drop, half-completed uploads abort. The mitigation is to **externalize state** to a shared store (Redis, DynamoDB) so any backend can serve any client — which eliminates the need for stickiness entirely.

Real-world deployments of stickiness cluster in three patterns. **Tomcat JSESSIONID** is the textbook Java pattern: the servlet container generates a `JSESSIONID` cookie, stores the `HttpSession` object in local memory, and the LB learns the cookie-to-backend mapping. The pattern works but creates operational headaches — the Tomcat cluster can't be elastically scaled without losing sessions, and a Tomcat restart logs out all its users. Modern Java deployments use Spring Session with Redis backing, eliminating the need for stickiness. **AWS ALB sticky cookies** support two modes: `lb_cookie` (ALB generates and manages the cookie, default duration 1 day, max 7 days) and `app_cookie` (ALB uses an application-provided cookie name). The ALB's stickiness is per-target-group: enabling it on a target group causes the ALB to route repeat clients to the same target within that group. **WebSocket load-balancing** essentially requires stickiness for the lifetime of the connection (the WS handshake lands on one backend, and subsequent frames must too) — but most L7 balancers handle this at the connection level rather than via cookies, since a WS upgrade is one TCP connection. HAProxy's `stick-table` and NGINX's `ip_hash` and `hash $cookie_JSESSIONID` directives cover the same patterns.

The decision to use sticky sessions should be a **last resort, not a default**. The proper architecture for most modern services is stateless backends + externalized state (Redis, DynamoDB, database) — this enables free elastic scaling, even load balancing, zero client-visible failures on backend restart, and the full benefit of RR/LC distribution. Stickiness is appropriate when (a) the state cannot be externalized cheaply (e.g., a long-lived WebSocket connection's per-frame context, a video transcode job's intermediate buffers), (b) the application is legacy and cannot be refactored to externalize state, or (c) the performance cost of externalizing state is too high (e.g., reading session from Redis adds 1ms to every request, and the service runs at 1ms p99). Even in those cases, the stickiness window should be as short as possible (e.g., sticky only for the duration of a checkout flow, not for the user's lifetime) to minimize the uneven-load and failover-loss impact. The architectural pattern is: externalize what you can, use stickiness for what you can't, monitor the uneven-load distribution, and have a failover story for when a sticky backend dies.

A subtle operational concern is **stale stickiness entries**. When a backend is removed (failed or scaled down), its sticky mappings in the LB's table become orphaned — the LB doesn't know the backend is gone until it tries to route and fails. Clients with the stale cookie get routed to the dead backend, fail, retry, and the LB eventually learns to route them elsewhere. Modern balancers (HAProxy `stick-table`, AWS ALB) automatically expire stale mappings when the backend's health-check fails, but there's a window of failed requests during the transition. The mitigation: short stickiness TTLs (minutes, not days) so stale mappings age out fast, and graceful drain on backend removal so in-flight requests complete. Another concern is **cookie manipulation** by clients — a malicious client could set `SERVERID=backend1` to deliberately overload one backend, or cycle through SERVERID values to defeat stickiness. Production balancers sign or encrypt the sticky cookie (HAProxy `httponly`, `secure`, `secret` options) to prevent this.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Client (new) participant LB as Load Balancer
(sticky) participant B1 as Backend 1
(has session for client) participant B2 as Backend 2 Note over C,LB: First request (no cookie yet) C->>LB: GET /cart (no Cookie header) LB->>LB: pick backend by RR -> B1 LB->>B1: forward request B1->>B1: create session, store cart B1-->>LB: 200 OK, Set-Cookie: SESSIONID=abc, backend=B1 LB-->>C: 200 OK + Set-Cookie Note over C,LB: Second request (cookie present) C->>LB: GET /cart (Cookie: SESSIONID=abc, backend=B1) LB->>LB: read cookie -> B1 LB->>B1: forward (B1 has the session) B1-->>LB: 200 OK, cart contents LB-->>C: 200 OK Note over C,LB: If B1 fails... C->>LB: GET /cart (Cookie: backend=B1) LB->>LB: B1 unhealthy -> re-route to B2 LB->>B2: forward (B2 has NO session) B2-->>LB: 200 OK, empty cart <- STATE LOST LB-->>C: 200 OK + Set-Cookie: backend=B2 (new pin) ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` COOKIE-BASED STICKINESS: client LB backends | | +----+ | GET /cart | +---------->| B1 | (has cart) | (no cookie) | | +----+ |--------------------->| | | | RR ->| pick B1 +----+ | | +---------->| B2 | (idle) | | +----+ |<---------------------| 200 + Set-Cookie: SID=abc; BE=B1 | cart | | | (next request) | | GET /cart | | Cookie: SID=abc; BE=B1 |--------------------->| read BE=B1 -> forward to B1 |<---------------------| 200 cart contents IP-HASH STICKINESS: client (10.0.0.5) ----hash(10.0.0.5) % N = 2----> B2 client (10.0.0.5) ----hash(10.0.0.5) % N = 2----> B2 (always B2) problem: corporate NAT 1000 users behind 1 public IP -> all hash to same backend -> SATURATED +------+ +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ | 10.0 |---+ | | | | | | | .0.5 | +-->| LB |------>| B1 | | B2 | (idle) +------+ | |hash | |HOT! | | | +------+ | +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ | 10.0 |---+ ^ | .0.6 | | (same source IP after NAT) +------+ | ... 1000 users behind same NAT ``` ### Walkthrough 1. On the client's first request, the LB sees no sticky cookie (or no recognizable session ID). It picks a backend using its normal algorithm (RR, LC, WRR) — say backend B1 — and forwards the request. The backend processes it and may create server-side state (session, cart, upload). 2. On the response, the LB injects (or passes through) a cookie identifying the chosen backend — either a balancer-generated cookie (`SERVERID=B1`) or the application's own session cookie (`JSESSIONID=abc`) which the LB has learned to associate with B1. The client stores the cookie. 3. On subsequent requests, the client sends the cookie. The LB reads it, looks up the backend mapping, and routes to the same backend — preserving the server-side state. If that backend has failed (health check), the LB re-routes to a healthy backend and updates the cookie — but the server-side state is lost unless it was externalized.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Sticky-session load balancer using cookie or IP hash.
# Demonstrates: cookie-based stickiness with failover, IP-hash with
# consistent hashing, and the state-loss failure mode.

import hashlib
import threading
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Backend:
    name: str
    healthy: bool = True

class StickyCookieLB:
    """Cookie-based stickiness. First request: RR pick + set-cookie.
    Subsequent: read cookie, route to same backend. Failover: re-pick
    and update cookie, but server-side state is LOST."""

    def __init__(self, backends: list[Backend], cookie_name="SERVERID"):
        self.backends = backends
        self.cookie_name = cookie_name
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._rr = 0

    def pick(self, cookie_value: str | None = None) -> tuple[Backend, str]:
        """Returns (backend, new_cookie_value_or_None).
        Cookie value is the backend name (in production: signed/encrypted)."""
        with self._lock:
            # 1. Try to honor existing stickiness
            if cookie_value:
                for b in self.backends:
                    if b.name == cookie_value and b.healthy:
                        return b, None   # sticky hit, no cookie change
                # sticky miss: backend gone or unhealthy -> re-pick
            # 2. New client (or failover): RR pick among healthy
            healthy = [b for b in self.backends if b.healthy]
            if not healthy:
                raise RuntimeError("no healthy backends")
            chosen = healthy[self._rr % len(healthy)]
            self._rr += 1
            return chosen, chosen.name   # set-cookie with backend name

class IPHashLB:
    """IP-hash stickiness. hash(client_ip) % N -> deterministic backend.
    No cookie needed, but breaks under NAT (all clients same IP)."""

    def __init__(self, backends: list[Backend]):
        self.backends = backends

    def pick(self, client_ip: str) -> Backend:
        healthy = [b for b in self.backends if b.healthy]
        if not healthy:
            raise RuntimeError("no healthy backends")
        # Consistent hashing would use a ring; here we use simple mod
        h = int(hashlib.md5(client_ip.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
        return healthy[h % len(healthy)]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    backends = [Backend("B1"), Backend("B2"), Backend("B3")]
    lb = StickyCookieLB(backends)

    # Client 1: first request (no cookie)
    b, cookie = lb.pick(None)
    print(f"Client1 req1: backend={b.name}, set-cookie=SERVERID={cookie}")

    # Client 1: second request (with cookie, should stick to B1)
    b, cookie = lb.pick("B1")
    print(f"Client1 req2: backend={b.name}, cookie_change={cookie}")
    # Expected: B1, None (sticky hit, no cookie change)

    # Failover: B1 dies
    backends[0].healthy = False
    b, cookie = lb.pick("B1")
    print(f"Client1 req3 (B1 down): backend={b.name}, set-cookie={cookie}")
    print(f"  -> server-side state LOST (B2 doesn't have Client1's session)")
    # Expected: B2 or B3 (RR re-pick), new cookie value

    # IP-hash demo
    ip_lb = IPHashLB(backends)
    for ip in ["10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.3"]:
        print(f"IP {ip} -> {ip_lb.pick(ip).name}")
    # 10.0.0.1 always maps to same backend (sticky)
```

quiz.explanation: Consistent hashing (Karger et al., 1997) is a hashing scheme where adding or removing a backend re-maps only 1/N of clients, not 100%. The naive hash(client) % N is brittle: change N (add a backend) and every client's modulo changes, breaking all stickiness. Consistent hashing places both backends and clients on a virtual ring (0 to 2^32); each client is served by the next backend clockwise on the ring.
